reconcile.connective: Henry treats the two forms as one substance in two functions — the same voice serving as public notification to John and a direct answer to Jesus's own prayer.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the difference as real: Mark's voice addresses Jesus privately, while Matthew's third-person wording announces him publicly to the crowd.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: Jesus, Interrupted: Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible (and Why We Don't Know About Them)
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, Jesus, Interrupted (HarperOne, 2009), pp. 39-40

excerpts.excerpt_text: Here, and in Mark, it is expressed as spoken to Christ; in Matthew as spoken of him: This is my beloved Son. It comes all to one; it was intended to be a notification to John, and as such was properly expressed by, This is my beloved Son; and likewise an answer to his prayer, and so it is most fitly expressed by. Thou art.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly names both forms of the heavenly voice (Matthew's third-person 'This is' vs Mark/Luke's second-person 'Thou art') and argues they are one substance suited to two different narrative purposes, which is precisely this contradiction's tension.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley lists Matt. 3:17, Mark 1:11, and Luke 3:22 verbatim side by side under the heading 'Forms of report. Different.' (Doctrinal Discrepancies, pp. 153-154) and concludes that 'in each the fundamental idea is preserved under all the various forms ... precisely what the sacred writers intended.'
